angle: from $0 to $100k, every step in order
title: From $0 to $100K: Every Step, In Order

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. Getting from zero to one hundred thousand dollars is the hardest climb in personal finance. Charlie Munger famously said the first hundred thousand is the hardest. But here's what almost nobody tells you. There's an order to it. Do the steps in the right order, and every step makes the next one easier. Do them in the wrong order, and you can work hard for years and barely move.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: Getting from zero to one hundred thousand dollars has an order. Most people do it backwards.

scenes.text: From zero to one hundred thousand dollars. Twelve steps, in order. Each one builds the floor for the next.

Most people do it backwards. They start investing before they have any cash for emergencies, so the first surprise bill sends them to a credit card. Or they pay off a low interest loan early while their high interest card grows. Or they skip free money from their employer because they think they can't afford to save. Each mistake alone costs a little. Together, they cost years.
scenes.caption: MOST PEOPLE DO IT BACKWARDS

scenes.text: Today we'll go step by step, in order, from the very first dollar to one hundred thousand. And we'll look at the whole journey from three angles. First the numbers: how long it really takes. Then the psychology: why most people quit around the same point. And then the playbook: three real paths for three different incomes.
scenes.caption: 12 STEPS, 3 ANGLES

scenes.text: If you're starting from zero, or even below zero, this video is for you. Let's go.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our numbers come from named sources. Household savings data comes from the Federal Reserve's survey on the economic well being of U.S. households. Net worth data comes from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances. Credit card rates come from the Federal Reserve's consumer credit report. Retirement account rules come from the IRS, and the limits change every year, so always check the current numbers.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: Growth examples use a seven percent average yearly return, compounded monthly, as an illustration. That's not a promise. Markets go up and down, sometimes a lot. This is education, not financial advice. Use it as a map, and adjust it to your own life.
scenes.query: Calculator and pen on financial papers
scenes.caption: EDUCATION, NOT ADVICE

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Before the steps, let's see exactly how long the climb takes, because once you see the math, it stops feeling impossible.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: At a seven percent illustration, investing five hundred dollars a month gets you to one hundred thousand dollars in about eleven years. One thousand a month gets you there in under seven.

card.note: Illustration at 7% a year, compounded monthly. Not guaranteed.

scenes.text: Notice something. Doubling your monthly amount doesn't cut the time in half. It cuts it from about eleven years to under seven. That's because at the start, almost all of the balance is your own money. Growth only becomes big later. At five hundred a month, you'd put in about sixty six thousand of your own money, and growth adds the rest.
scenes.caption: YOUR MONEY DOES MOST OF IT

scenes.text: Flip it around. If you want one hundred thousand dollars in ten years, you'd need to invest about five hundred eighty dollars a month. In seven years, about nine hundred twenty five. In five years, about fourteen hundred.

card.note: Illustration at 7% a year, compounded monthly. Not guaranteed.

scenes.text: Those numbers might look big. But remember, they don't have to come only from cutting costs. Employer matches count. Raises count. A paid off car loan that you redirect counts. Most people who reach one hundred thousand do it with a mix of all of those, not with one heroic budget.
scenes.caption: EVERYTHING COUNTS

scenes.text: Now here's where most people actually start. The Federal Reserve found that sixty three percent of adults would cover a surprise four hundred dollar expense with cash or its equivalent. That means more than a third couldn't. And credit card interest rates, according to the Federal Reserve, have been above twenty percent. So for many people, step zero is simply stopping the bleeding.
scenes.caption: WHERE MOST PEOPLE START

scenes.text: One more number before the steps: the cost of waiting. If you put off starting for just three years, you don't arrive three years later at the same place. You lose the three years of growth at the very end, when the balance is largest. That's why the best time to start this road is always now, even with a small amount. Twenty five dollars a month started today often beats two hundred dollars a month started someday.
scenes.caption: THE COST OF WAITING

scenes.text: And the last number is the one that makes all the others work: consistency. A plan you follow for ten years at five hundred dollars a month beats a plan for one thousand a month that you abandon after eighteen months. When you choose your monthly amount, choose one you can keep through a bad month, not just a good one. You can always raise it later.
scenes.caption: CONSISTENCY BEATS SIZE

scenes.text: Okay. Now the twelve steps, in order. Step one takes about one evening, and it changes everything after it.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Step one. Know your numbers. You can't plan a trip without knowing where you're starting.
scenes.caption: STEP 1

scenes.text: Two numbers matter. Your net worth, which is everything you own minus everything you owe. And your monthly cash flow, which is what comes in minus what goes out. Most people have never written either of them down. They have a feeling about their money, and feelings are usually wrong, in both directions.
scenes.caption: TWO NUMBERS

scenes.text: Here's how. Open every account: checking, savings, retirement, credit cards, loans. Write down each balance. Add up what you own, subtract what you owe. Then look at the last three months of bank statements and calculate your average income and spending. It takes one evening. It's not fun. But it's the foundation of everything else.
scenes.caption: ONE EVENING

scenes.text: Say you discover your net worth is minus eight thousand dollars, and you have two hundred dollars left at the end of a typical month. That's not bad news. That's a starting line. You now know exactly how much fuel you have, two hundred dollars a month, and exactly how far you have to go. People who track their numbers tend to make better decisions, simply because they can see them.
scenes.caption: A STARTING LINE

scenes.text: Step two. Build a small emergency fund, around one thousand to two thousand dollars, before anything else.

card.title: A starter emergency fund
card.sub: one thousand to two thousand dollars

scenes.caption: STEP 2

scenes.text: Why first? Because without it, every surprise becomes new debt. The flat tire, the dentist, the broken phone. If you put that on a card at over twenty percent, you're going backwards. A small cushion breaks that cycle. It's not meant to cover a job loss yet. It's meant to cover the normal chaos of life.
scenes.query: Car with flat tire on road
scenes.caption: LIFE IS CHAOS

scenes.text: Open a separate savings account, ideally at a different bank, so it's not sitting next to your spending money. Set an automatic transfer on payday. Sell a few things you don't use. Pick up a few extra shifts. The goal is speed. Most people can build this in one to four months if they focus.
scenes.caption: SPEED MATTERS

scenes.text: Here's what changes. The next time the car needs a three hundred dollar repair, you pay it from the cushion, and then refill it. No new debt. No panic. It sounds small, but for many people this is the first time money feels like it's working for them instead of against them.
scenes.caption: NO NEW DEBT

scenes.text: Step three. If your employer matches retirement contributions, contribute enough to get the full match.

card.title: Get the full employer match
card.sub: free money comes before debt payoff

scenes.caption: STEP 3
scenes.chapter: Step 3. Get the full employer match

scenes.text: Why this comes before paying off debt: a match is often a fifty or one hundred percent instant return on your money. A common formula is fifty cents for every dollar you put in, up to six percent of your salary. No investment and no debt payoff beats an instant fifty percent return. Skipping it is turning down part of your pay.
scenes.caption: FREE MONEY

scenes.text: Look up your plan's matching rule in your benefits portal, or ask HR. Then set your contribution to at least the level that gets every matching dollar. If money is tight, start at whatever you can, and raise it by one percent every few months until you reach the full match.
scenes.caption: ASK HR TODAY

scenes.text: Say you earn fifty thousand dollars and your employer matches fifty percent up to six percent. You put in three thousand a year. Your employer adds fifteen hundred. That's fifteen hundred dollars a year you'd lose by not participating, and over thirty years, with growth, that alone could add up to far more than you'd expect.
scenes.caption: $1,500 A YEAR FREE

scenes.text: Step four. Pay off high interest debt, especially credit cards.
scenes.caption: STEP 4
scenes.short_hook: Paying the minimum on a credit card is treading water. Here's how to escape.

scenes.text: Credit card balances often charge over twenty percent a year. Paying off a card at twenty two percent is like earning a guaranteed twenty two percent return. Nothing in the investing world reliably beats that. So until high interest debt is gone, it's the best investment you have.
scenes.caption: OVER 20% A YEAR

scenes.text: There are two popular methods. The avalanche: pay minimums on everything, and throw every extra dollar at the highest interest rate first. It saves the most money. The snowball: pay off the smallest balance first for quick wins. It can keep you motivated. Either works far better than paying minimums on everything. Pick the one you'll actually stick to.
scenes.caption: AVALANCHE OR SNOWBALL

scenes.text: Say you have three cards, with balances of two thousand, four thousand and six thousand dollars. With the avalanche method, you'd target whichever card has the highest rate, while paying minimums on the others. When it's gone, that whole payment rolls into the next one. Each payoff speeds up the next. People often describe the last card as the fastest one, because by then they're throwing everything at it.
scenes.caption: ROLL IT FORWARD

scenes.text: Step five. Grow your emergency fund to three to six months of essential expenses.

card.title: A full emergency fund
card.sub: three to six months of essentials

scenes.caption: STEP 5

scenes.text: Your starter fund protects you from small surprises. This one protects you from big ones: a job loss, a medical problem, a family emergency. With three to six months of essentials saved, a layoff becomes a hard time instead of a financial disaster. And it means you'll never have to sell investments at a bad time to pay rent.
scenes.caption: BIG SURPRISES

scenes.text: Add up your essential monthly costs: housing, food, utilities, insurance, transport, minimum payments. Multiply by three to six. If your income is very stable, three might be enough. If you're self employed or your industry is unpredictable, aim closer to six. Keep it in a high yield savings account that's FDIC insured.
scenes.caption: 3 TO 6 MONTHS

scenes.text: Say your essentials are three thousand dollars a month. Your target is somewhere between nine and eighteen thousand dollars. That sounds like a lot. But if you just finished paying off debt, you already have a monthly payment habit. Keep making the same payment, just to yourself. Many people fill this fund faster than they paid off their debt.
scenes.caption: PAY YOURSELF

scenes.text: Step six. Automate your saving and push your savings rate toward fifteen to twenty percent.
scenes.caption: STEP 6
scenes.chapter: Step 6. Automate and raise your rate

scenes.text: Willpower runs out. Automation doesn't. When money moves to savings and investments automatically on payday, before you see it, you adjust your spending to what's left. That's the single most reliable way people build wealth on ordinary incomes. And your savings rate, the share of your income you keep, decides how fast you climb.
scenes.caption: AUTOMATION WINS

scenes.text: Set up automatic contributions to your retirement account through payroll, and automatic transfers to your other accounts on payday. Then use a simple rule: every time you get a raise, send at least half of it to savings. Your lifestyle still improves, but your rate climbs every year without it ever feeling like a sacrifice.
scenes.caption: HALF OF EVERY RAISE

scenes.text: Say you earn sixty thousand dollars and save five percent. That's three thousand a year. Each year you get a three percent raise and send half of it to savings. After about seven years, without ever cutting your spending, you're saving well over ten percent. That's the quiet power of automating your raises.
scenes.caption: THE RATE CLIMBS

scenes.text: Quick pause. If you're finding this step by step useful, subscribe to the channel. I'm making a full series on every stage, from zero to one million, and subscribing is the best way not to miss the next step. Now, step seven.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Step seven. Open an individual retirement account, an IRA, alongside your workplace plan.

card.title: Open an IRA
card.sub: a retirement account of your own

scenes.caption: STEP 7

scenes.text: An IRA is a retirement account you open yourself, at a brokerage. There are two main types. A traditional IRA may give you a tax deduction now, and you pay tax later. A Roth IRA uses money you've already paid tax on, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax free. Both let your investments grow without yearly taxes on gains.
scenes.caption: TRADITIONAL OR ROTH

scenes.text: Which one? Many people early in their careers, in lower tax brackets, prefer the Roth, because they pay tax now at a lower rate. Income limits apply to Roth contributions, and the yearly limits change, so check the current IRS rules. Open the account, set up an automatic monthly contribution, and, this is important, actually choose an investment inside it. Money sitting as cash in an IRA doesn't grow much.
scenes.caption: CHOOSE AN INVESTMENT

scenes.text: That last point catches a lot of people. They open an IRA, transfer money in, and never pick an investment. Years later, they discover it's been sitting in cash, earning almost nothing. Try this: if you already have an IRA, log in today and check what it's actually invested in.
scenes.caption: CHECK IT TODAY

scenes.text: Step eight. Invest simply. Broad, low cost index funds.
scenes.caption: STEP 8

scenes.text: An index fund buys a whole market, like the five hundred largest U.S. companies, or the entire U.S. stock market, instead of trying to pick winners. Research, like S and P's long running SPIVA reports, has repeatedly found that most actively managed funds trail their benchmark index over long periods, especially after fees.
scenes.query: New York Stock Exchange trading floor
scenes.caption: BUY THE WHOLE MARKET

scenes.text: A simple approach many investors use is one or two broad stock index funds, plus a bond fund that grows as you get closer to needing the money. Or a single target date fund that does that mix for you. Look for low expense ratios. The less you pay, the more you keep. And keep it boring. Boring is the point.
scenes.caption: KEEP IT BORING

scenes.text: Here's why cost matters so much on the way to one hundred thousand. A fund charging one percent a year versus one charging a small fraction of a percent might not look different in year one. But over decades, that fee difference compounds into a very large amount of money. Same market, same years, less money for you.
scenes.caption: LOW COST WINS

scenes.text: Step nine. Control the big three: housing, transportation and food.
scenes.caption: STEP 9

scenes.text: According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, housing, transportation and food together make up the largest share of what American households spend. That means a ten percent cut in one of these is worth more than cancelling dozens of small subscriptions. Small savings help. The big three move the needle.
scenes.caption: THE BIG THREE

scenes.text: On housing, think about a roommate, a smaller place, or a slightly longer commute. On transportation, keep cars longer, buy reliable used ones, and avoid long loans. On food, cook more and plan meals. You don't need to do all of it. One meaningful change in one of the big three can free hundreds of dollars a month.
scenes.caption: KEEP THE CAR

scenes.text: Say you keep your current car for four more years instead of trading it in for a new one with a six hundred dollar payment. That's over twenty eight thousand dollars you don't spend. Invested instead, that money alone could cover a big chunk of the road to one hundred thousand.
scenes.caption: COOK MORE

scenes.text: Step ten. Grow your income. Cutting has a floor. Earning has no ceiling.
scenes.caption: STEP 10

scenes.text: There's only so much you can cut. But there's no limit to how much your income can grow. A raise, a promotion, a new job, a certification, or a side income can change your timeline more than any budget. Studies of wage growth have found that people who switch jobs often see bigger raises than people who stay.
scenes.caption: NO CEILING

scenes.text: Start with your current job. Ask what it takes to get to the next level, and get it in writing. Look at job listings for your role to see what you're worth. Learn one skill that's in demand in your field. And if you have time, a side income, even a few hundred dollars a month, can go straight to savings.
scenes.caption: KNOW YOUR WORTH

scenes.text: Say a new certification bumps your salary by six thousand dollars a year. If you invest all of it, that's five hundred dollars a month. At a seven percent illustration, that alone gets to one hundred thousand in about eleven years. One skill, one raise, one decision.
scenes.caption: ONE SKILL, ONE RAISE

scenes.text: Step eleven. Beat lifestyle creep.
scenes.caption: STEP 11

scenes.text: Lifestyle creep is when your spending rises as fast as your income. A bigger apartment, a nicer car, more eating out. None of it feels crazy. Each upgrade feels earned. But if everything you gain gets spent, your net worth stands still, no matter how much you earn. It's why some high earners never get anywhere.
scenes.caption: LIFESTYLE CREEP

scenes.text: The fix isn't to never upgrade. It's to upgrade on purpose. Pick the one or two things that genuinely make you happier, and spend on those without guilt. Then keep everything else the same. And keep the half of every raise rule from step six. Your life gets better, and your savings rate keeps climbing.
scenes.caption: UPGRADE ON PURPOSE

scenes.text: Picture two coworkers who each get a ten thousand dollar raise. One upgrades their car and apartment and ends the year with the same savings as before. The other upgrades their apartment a little and invests five thousand. Ten years later, the second coworker could have roughly seventy thousand dollars more, at a seven percent illustration, from that single decision repeated each year.
scenes.caption: SAME RAISE, NEW RESULT

scenes.text: Step twelve. Stay the course. This is the step that decides whether you actually reach one hundred thousand.
scenes.caption: STEP 12

scenes.text: Somewhere on the way, the market will drop. Maybe ten percent, maybe thirty. Broad markets have fallen like that many times in history and, so far, recovered, though the past doesn't guarantee the future. The people who reach their goals usually keep investing through the drops. The people who don't often sell at the bottom and lock in their losses.
scenes.query: Stock market chart falling on screen
scenes.caption: THE MARKET WILL DROP

scenes.text: Make a simple rule now, while things are calm. I keep investing every month, no matter what the news says. Check your accounts once a month, not once a day. And once a year, rebalance: if your stocks have grown much bigger than your plan, move a bit back to bonds, and vice versa. That's it. Discipline beats intelligence.
scenes.caption: ONE RULE

scenes.text: Think of it this way. When prices fall, your monthly investment buys more shares. If you're still years away from needing the money, a drop is actually a sale. It doesn't feel like one. It feels terrible. But the investors who treat drops as sales, instead of emergencies, are usually the ones who get to one hundred thousand first.
scenes.caption: A DROP IS A SALE

scenes.text: Every path starts with finding some money each month. So here's where people usually find their first three hundred dollars a month, without a second job.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Start with subscriptions and memberships. Streaming services, apps, a gym you don't go to, software you forgot about. Go through your bank statement line by line. Many people find thirty to eighty dollars a month here in under an hour, and they don't miss any of it.
scenes.caption: SUBSCRIPTIONS

scenes.text: Next, the bills you never question. Call your phone company, your internet provider and your insurance company, and ask for a better rate, or compare quotes from competitors. Prices for the same service can vary a lot, and loyal customers are often paying the most. An hour of phone calls can save another fifty to one hundred fifty dollars a month.
scenes.caption: CALL AND ASK

scenes.text: Then food. Delivery apps add fees, tips and higher menu prices on top of the meal. Cutting delivery from twice a week to twice a month, and bringing lunch to work a few days a week, can easily free up one hundred dollars or more. You're not giving up good food. You're giving up the markup.
scenes.caption: THE FOOD MARKUP

scenes.text: And finally, the money you already have but don't see. A tax refund. A bonus. Cash back rewards. Money from selling things you don't use. Instead of letting these disappear into everyday spending, send them straight to your current step. A single tax refund can fill a starter emergency fund in one day.
scenes.caption: MONEY YOU DON'T SEE

scenes.text: Add those up, and three hundred dollars a month is realistic for a lot of households, with no change in where you live or what you drive. At a seven percent illustration, three hundred dollars a month for thirty years grows to over three hundred sixty thousand dollars. That's what's hiding in your bank statement right now.
scenes.caption: $300 A MONTH = A LOT

scenes.text: Angle two. The psychology. Because most people who start this journey don't fail at step one. They quit somewhere in the middle. And it happens at surprisingly predictable points.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: Most people quit saving at almost exactly the same point. Here's why.

scenes.text: The first danger zone is around ten to twenty thousand dollars. The debt is gone, there's a cushion, and the urgency disappears. People feel safe, and safe feels like done. This is where many people stop pushing. The fix is to set the next goal before you reach the current one. When you hit twenty thousand, you should already be aiming at fifty.
scenes.caption: DANGER ZONE 1: SAFE FEELS DONE

scenes.text: The second danger zone is the slow middle, around thirty to sixty thousand. Growth is still small compared with your contributions, and every month feels the same. It's boring. Behavioral researchers have shown that people value rewards now much more than rewards later. When the reward is years away, motivation fades. The fix is to celebrate milestones: every ten thousand dollars, mark it. Make progress visible.
scenes.caption: DANGER ZONE 2: THE SLOW MIDDLE

scenes.text: The third danger zone is comparison. Around the time you're making real progress, you'll notice what other people are spending. New cars, big trips, bigger houses. It's easy to feel like you're missing out. But remember, you're seeing their spending, not their balance sheet. Many of them are on level two, with nicer things.
scenes.caption: DANGER ZONE 3: COMPARISON

scenes.text: The fourth is the first big market drop. Watching ten thousand dollars disappear from your account in a few weeks is genuinely painful. Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains feel good. That's why people panic. Knowing this in advance won't remove the pain, but it can stop you from acting on it.
scenes.caption: DANGER ZONE 4: THE FIRST CRASH

scenes.text: And here's the good news. People who reach one hundred thousand often say the second hundred thousand came much faster. Partly because of compounding. But partly because by then, saving had become a habit, not a decision. The first hundred thousand builds the person. After that, the person builds the money.
scenes.caption: THE HABIT BUILDS THE MONEY

scenes.text: Angle three. The playbook. Here are three example paths to one hundred thousand dollars, for three different incomes. They're made up examples, but the math is simple and real.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: Three incomes, three paths to one hundred thousand dollars. Which one is yours?

scenes.text: Path one. Forty thousand dollars a year. Alex starts with three thousand dollars of credit card debt. Six months to build a starter cushion and clear the card. Then Alex invests three hundred dollars a month, plus a small employer match of about one hundred dollars. Every raise, half goes to savings. At a seven percent illustration, Alex reaches one hundred thousand in roughly thirteen years. Not fast. But steady, and completely realistic.
scenes.caption: PATH 1: $40,000 A YEAR

scenes.text: Path two. Seventy thousand dollars a year. Jordan has no debt except a car loan. Jordan builds a full emergency fund in a year, then invests fifteen percent of income, about eight hundred seventy five dollars a month, plus a match of about one hundred seventy five. That's roughly one thousand fifty dollars a month. At the same illustration, Jordan reaches one hundred thousand in a little over six years.
scenes.caption: PATH 2: $70,000 A YEAR

scenes.text: Path three. A couple earning one hundred twenty thousand together. Sam and Riley keep one modest car, cook most meals, and invest twenty percent of their income, about two thousand dollars a month, including matches. At a seven percent illustration, they reach one hundred thousand dollars in a little under four years. Then they keep going, and the second hundred thousand comes even faster.
scenes.caption: PATH 3: $120,000 TOGETHER

scenes.text: Notice what's the same in all three paths. The order. Starter cushion, match, high interest debt, full cushion, automate, invest cheaply, control the big three, grow income, beat lifestyle creep, stay the course. The income changes the speed. The order is the same for everyone.
scenes.caption: THE ORDER IS THE SAME

scenes.text: And here's your one page plan. At the top, write your net worth today. Under it, write which step you're on. Under that, the one action for this month. And at the bottom, the date you'll check again. Tape it somewhere you'll see it. That page is worth more than any budgeting app, because it tells you exactly what to do next.
scenes.caption: YOUR ONE PAGE PLAN

scenes.text: Let's walk the whole road from zero to one hundred thousand, milestone by milestone, and talk about what actually changes at each one. Because knowing what's coming makes it much easier to keep going.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: Here's what one thousand, ten thousand and fifty thousand dollars really feel like.

scenes.text: One thousand dollars. This is the first milestone, and it's mostly emotional. For many people, it's the first time they've ever had money that wasn't already spoken for. A surprise bill no longer means a credit card. People often describe a strange, quiet feeling of control. It's small money. It's a big moment.
scenes.caption: $1,000: CONTROL

scenes.text: Ten thousand dollars. Now you have real options. You could survive a few months of reduced income. You could move for a better job. You could say no to something that's bad for you. Ten thousand dollars is often the point where people stop feeling poor, even if their income hasn't changed at all. And at a seven percent illustration, ten thousand dollars can grow by about seven hundred dollars in a year, without you adding a cent.
scenes.caption: $10,000: OPTIONS

scenes.text: Twenty five thousand dollars. This is where many people's emergency fund is full and their investing is truly under way. You can absorb most of life's surprises. And it's often where people first notice their investments moving by more in a single day than they used to save in a week. That can be exciting, and a little scary. It's a good time to remind yourself that daily swings don't matter. Years matter.
scenes.caption: $25,000: REAL INVESTOR

scenes.text: Fifty thousand dollars. Halfway. But here's the surprise: in time, you're usually more than halfway, because the second fifty thousand comes faster than the first. Growth starts to carry real weight. At a seven percent illustration, fifty thousand dollars can earn around three thousand five hundred in a year. For many people that's like an extra month or two of saving, delivered by the market instead of their paycheck.
scenes.caption: $50,000: HALFWAY

scenes.text: Seventy five thousand dollars. This is where the finish line becomes visible, and where a lot of people get impatient. They start looking for ways to speed up, and that's when risky bets look tempting. Don't. You're close precisely because you did boring things consistently. Keep doing them. The last stretch rewards patience more than any other.
scenes.caption: $75,000: STAY PATIENT

scenes.text: And one hundred thousand dollars. Most people say it doesn't feel like fireworks. It feels like confidence. You've proven to yourself that you can do it. You know the steps. And the next milestones, two hundred and fifty thousand, five hundred thousand, one million, suddenly stop sounding like fantasy and start sounding like math.
scenes.caption: $100,000: CONFIDENCE

scenes.text: Before the recap, five mistakes that slow people down on the way to one hundred thousand.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Mistake one. Investing before having any emergency cash. The first surprise turns into credit card debt, and the whole plan stalls. Mistake two. Paying off low interest debt early while ignoring high interest debt. Always attack the highest rate first. Mistake three. Leaving money in cash inside a retirement account, never actually invested.
scenes.caption: MISTAKES 1 TO 3

scenes.text: Mistake four. Chasing fast money. Hot stock tips, crypto hype, a friend's sure thing. Some people get lucky. Many lose years of progress. And mistake five. Stopping contributions when the market drops, which means buying less when prices are lowest. Keep the automation running. The plan works because you don't interrupt it.
scenes.caption: MISTAKES 4 AND 5

scenes.text: Let me answer a few questions I get all the time about the first one hundred thousand.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Question one. Does home equity count toward the hundred thousand? For net worth, yes. But for this plan, I'd focus on savings and investments, because that's money that can grow and support you. Question two. Should I invest or pay off student loans first? It depends on the rate. Low rate federal loans can often sit alongside investing. High rate private loans usually come first.
scenes.caption: HOME EQUITY? STUDENT LOANS?

scenes.text: Question three. What if I'm starting at forty five? The steps are the same. You'll probably invest larger amounts, and you can use catch up contributions once you turn fifty, which the IRS allows in retirement accounts. Question four. What if my income is unpredictable? Build a bigger emergency fund, closer to six months, and invest a percentage of each payment instead of a fixed amount.
scenes.caption: STARTING LATE? IRREGULAR INCOME?

scenes.text: Question five. Do I need a financial advisor to do this? Most people can do these twelve steps on their own. If you want help, a fee only planner who charges by the hour or by the project can review your plan without selling you products. Just make sure you know exactly how anyone you work with gets paid.
scenes.caption: DO I NEED AN ADVISOR?

scenes.text: Question six. Where should I keep my emergency fund? Somewhere safe, separate and easy to reach. For most people that means a high yield savings account at an FDIC insured bank, or a credit union insured by the NCUA. Not in stocks, because the emergency always seems to arrive when the market is down. Question seven. Is it okay to use a budgeting app? Absolutely, if you'll use it. The best budget is the one you actually look at.
scenes.caption: WHERE DOES THE CUSHION GO?

scenes.text: Question eight. What if I fall back a step? You will, probably more than once. A car dies, you change jobs, a family emergency eats your cushion. That's not failure. That's exactly what the cushion was for. Go back to the step you're on, rebuild, and keep going. The people who reach one hundred thousand aren't the ones who never fall back. They're the ones who never quit.
scenes.caption: WHAT IF I FALL BACK?

scenes.text: Let's recap the twelve steps, in order. One, know your numbers. Two, a starter emergency fund. Three, get the full employer match. Four, kill high interest debt. Five, a full emergency fund. Six, automate and raise your savings rate.
scenes.caption: STEPS 1 TO 6

scenes.text: Seven, open an IRA. Eight, invest simply and cheaply. Nine, control the big three. Ten, grow your income. Eleven, beat lifestyle creep. And twelve, stay the course. Do them in this order, and each step makes the next one easier.
scenes.caption: STEPS 7 TO 12

scenes.text: And the three angles. The numbers: five hundred a month gets there in about eleven years, one thousand in under seven. The psychology: watch out for the danger zones, especially safe feels done and the first crash. And the playbook: the income changes the speed, but the order stays the same for everyone.
scenes.caption: NUMBERS, PSYCHOLOGY, PLAYBOOK

scenes.text: And remember why the order matters so much. Each step protects the one after it. The starter cushion protects your debt payoff from new debt. The full cushion protects your investments from forced selling. Automation protects your plan from bad days and busy months. And staying the course protects all of it from fear. Skip a step, and the steps above it become fragile. Follow the order, and every step you climb stays climbed.
scenes.caption: EACH STEP PROTECTS THE NEXT

scenes.text: So here's your homework. Find your step. Just one. And do the action for that step this week. Not all twelve. One. Then next month, check where you are, and if that step is done, move to the next one. Twelve steps sounds like a lot, but you only ever have to do one at a time. If you want the full plan with worksheets, it's in my playbook, link in the description. And when you get close to one hundred thousand, watch my video on what changes at that level. I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
